260.title: Dhammas: the hindrances
260.hook: desire present, he knows; absent, he knows; how it arises, how it goes (MN 10)
260.howItsDone: Meditation teachers in a number of Buddhist traditions teach the five hindrances early, so that practitioners can recognize sensual desire, ill will, dullness, restlessness and doubt as passing states rather than personal failures.

segments.voice: Yesterday: knowing, and your line, just know it. Did you hold off fixing a mood for one full breath? Day two hundred sixty, and the fourth foundation.

Sit quietly for five minutes and the usual visitors tend to arrive. First the snack you suddenly want. Then irritation at the neighbor's leaf blower. Then a heavy, sleepy fog. Then a jittery itch to check your phone. And finally a little voice: is this even doing anything? It's tempting to read them as proof of being bad at meditation. The Buddha named them, all five, and made knowing them part of the practice. Today: dhammas, the hindrances.
screen: `THE SNACK, THE LEAF BLOWER, THE FOG.` → `IS THIS EVEN WORKING?` → `THE FIVE VISITORS, NAMED.`

segments.voice: The fourth foundation is called dhammas. It's a hard word here. It can mean teachings, or mental qualities, or the patterns the Buddha taught people to recognize in experience. The first pattern is the five hindrances, the nivaranas, things that cover over a clear mind. Sensual desire. Ill will. Sloth and torpor, that heavy, dull fog. Restlessness and worry. And doubt. For each one, the sutta gives the same five-part instruction. If desire is present in you, know that it's present. If it's absent, know that it's absent. Know how desire that hasn't arisen comes to arise. Know how desire that has arisen is let go of. And know how, once let go of, it doesn't come back in the future. Look at what that does. The hindrances aren't enemies to fight or proof that you're failing. They're patterns to study. When did the sleepiness come in? Right after lunch. What made it lift? Opening the window. When did the doubt show up? Right when things got boring. You become a kind of naturalist of your own mind, watching creatures arrive and leave. The Buddha elsewhere compares a mind free of the hindrances to someone out of debt, recovered from illness, released from prison, freed from slavery, and safely across a desert. That's the text's own picture of their going. But the first step is only this: it came, and it went.
screen: `DHAMMAS: PATTERNS TO RECOGNIZE.` · `FIVE HINDRANCES THAT COVER THE MIND.` · `PRESENT, ABSENT, ARISING, LETTING GO.` · `A NATURALIST OF YOUR OWN MIND.` · then, large: `IT CAME, IT WENT.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and rest with the breath. Wait for one of the five visitors to show up: wanting, irritation, dullness, restlessness, or doubt. When one arrives, name it: wanting is here. Watch it without chasing it away. Notice what it feels like, and, if you can, the moment it fades. Then name that too: wanting is gone. It came, it went. The bell holds the time.
Dhammas, the hindrances. Desire, ill will, dullness, restlessness and doubt: known when present, known when absent, watched as they come and go.
Your line: it came, it went. Today, catch one hindrance, maybe the afternoon slump or the itch to check your phone, and watch it come and go. Day two hundred sixty.

match.prompt: match each hindrance to how it shows up.

myth: having the hindrances means you're bad at meditation
the Buddha made knowing them part of the practice itself.
the sutta asks you to know a hindrance's absence as well as its presence
present, absent, arising, let go, and not returning.
the Buddha compares a mind free of hindrances to someone released from prison
also out of debt, recovered from illness, and safely across a desert.

fork.setup: ten minutes into a sit, doubt shows up: 'this is pointless.' what does the sutta ask?
options: get up; doubt means it's not working.
know it: doubt is present; watch how it arose and how it goes.
argue with the doubt until it's gone.
fork.reveal: doubt is one of the five hindrances. the instruction is to know it, study how it comes and goes, not to obey it or fight it.

original.note: Pali nīvaraṇa: a hindrance, something that covers over a clear mind.

trapdoor: what you thought: the hindrances are sins to feel guilty about.
what it means: five passing patterns that cover a clear mind, to be known as they come and go.
what a scholar hears: the similes of debt, illness, prison, slavery and the desert for the hindrances' absence appear in DN 2, the Sāmaññaphala Sutta.

261.title: Dhammas: the five heaps
261.howItsDone: The five aggregates are taught widely in Buddhist schools; practitioners contemplate them to see that each is changing and that no lasting, controlling self is found among them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dhammas, the hindrances. Five visitors, and your line was it came, it went. Which one showed up most? Day two hundred sixty-one.

Point to yourself. Go ahead. Where did your finger land? Maybe the middle of your chest. But is that you? Your chest is a body part. Your feelings are somewhere else. Your thoughts seem to be up in your head. Your memories aren't anywhere you can point to at all. We say I all day long, and it sounds like one solid thing. The Buddha suggested that if you look closely, what you call I comes apart into five heaps. Today's word: khandha.

Khandha means a heap, a bundle, a mass, like a bundle of sticks. The Buddha taught that what we call a person can be seen as five of them. Form, rupa: the body and the physical world. Feeling, vedana: pleasant, painful, neither, the second foundation. Perception, sanna: recognizing, labeling, that's a cup, that's my friend. Formations, sankhara: intentions, habits, the urges and choices that shape what we do. And consciousness, vinnana: the plain knowing of anything at all. In the Satipatthana Sutta, the instruction for each heap is familiar by now. Such is form, such is its arising, such is its passing away. The same for feeling, perception, formations and consciousness. Why sort yourself into heaps? Because in the Buddha's teaching, each heap, looked at closely, is changing all the time, and none of them, on its own, is a solid owner in charge of the rest. That's what the Buddha pointed to with the teaching of anatta, not-self. As it's usually taught, it isn't a claim that nobody is here. It's that a self of one piece, fixed and in control, isn't found in any of the five. Elsewhere the Buddha gives a set of pictures for them. Form is like a lump of foam on a river. Feeling like a bubble on the water. Perception like a mirage. Formations like the trunk of a banana tree, layer after layer and no hard core. And consciousness like a magician's trick.
screen: `KHANDHA: A HEAP, A BUNDLE.` · `WHAT WE CALL A PERSON: FIVE OF THEM.` · `EACH ONE ARISING AND PASSING.` · `FOAM, BUBBLE, MIRAGE, BANANA TREE, TRICK.` · then, large: `FIVE HEAPS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and pick one moment: a sound, like a car passing. Now sort it into five. Form: the sound waves, your ear. Feeling: pleasant, painful, or neither? Perception: the label, a car. Formations: any urge, wishing it would stop, wondering where it's going. Consciousness: the plain knowing of it all. Five heaps, one moment. Then let it go, and wait for the next one. The bell holds the time.
Khandha. A heap: the Buddha's five, form, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness, each one arising and passing.
Your line: five heaps. Today, when something upsets you, try sorting that one moment into five, and notice whether it feels a little less solid. Day two hundred sixty-one.

pairs: a lump of foam on a river
a banana tree with no hard core

it says a solid, controlling self isn't found in any of the five heaps.

like a bundle of sticks.

options: feeling.

fork.reveal: perception, sanna, is recognizing and labeling. the sound is form, its tone is feeling.

original.note: Pali khandha (Sanskrit skandha): a heap, bundle or aggregate.

trapdoor: what you thought: the five heaps are five parts of a person, like organs.
what it means: five ways experience comes together, each changing, none a solid owner.
what a scholar hears: the foam, bubble, mirage, banana trunk and magic-trick similes come from SN 22.95, the Pheṇapiṇḍūpama Sutta; the Sanskrit form skandha returns in the Heart Sutra.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikāya 10 (Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta), the five aggregates

262.title: Dhammas: the sense bases
262.hook: eye and forms, ear and sounds, and the fetter that arises with them (MN 10)
262.howItsDone: Buddhist monastics and lay practitioners practice 'guarding the sense doors': not avoiding sights and sounds, but noticing the wanting or aversion that arises with them before it takes hold.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was khandha, and your line was five heaps: form, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness. Did one upset feel less solid, sorted into five? Day two hundred sixty-two.

You're walking past a bakery, not hungry at all. Then the smell reaches you. Ten seconds later you're holding a cinnamon roll and wondering how it happened. Or you hear a certain song, and suddenly you're in a mood about someone you haven't thought of in years. It all started at a door: the nose, the ear. Something came in, and before you noticed, something hooked you. The sutta has a word for that hook. Today: dhammas, the sense bases.
screen: `THE BAKERY SMELL.` → `THE OLD SONG.` → `SOMETHING CAME IN AND HOOKED YOU.`

segments.voice: The sense bases, ayatana, come in six pairs. Eye and forms. Ear and sounds. Nose and smells. Tongue and tastes. Body and touches. And, the one the Buddhist tradition adds that English usually doesn't, mind and mind-objects: thoughts, memories, ideas, which the mind senses just as the eye senses color. For each pair the sutta gives the same instruction. The practitioner knows the eye, knows forms, and knows the fetter that arises dependent on both. Then, like yesterday with the hindrances: knows how an unarisen fetter arises, how an arisen fetter is let go of, and how it doesn't come back. A fetter, samyojana, is something that ties you, a knot or a chain. The eye isn't the problem. Neither is the bakery. The fetter is what arises where they meet: the little knot of wanting, or of pushing away, that ties you to what you saw or smelled. Picture each sense as a door of your house. Things will always walk up to the doors. That's life, and it's fine. The practice is to stand at the door and see what comes through with them: this sound came in, and a knot of irritation came in right behind it. Seen at the door, the fetter is still small. Seen twenty minutes later, you're already holding the cinnamon roll. Elsewhere the Buddha teaches what's called guarding the sense doors, close kin to this. As it's usually explained, it doesn't mean shutting them. It means being home when someone knocks.
screen: `SIX DOORS: EYE, EAR, NOSE, TONGUE, BODY, MIND.` · `THE FETTER ARISES WHERE THEY MEET.` · `STAND AT THE DOOR.` · `GUARDING, NOT SHUTTING.` · then, large: `THE FETTER AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably with eyes open or closed. Rest at the doors. Let sounds come in: know the sound, and see if anything comes with it, a like, a dislike. Let a smell or a touch come in the same way. Then notice a thought arriving at the mind's door. For each one, just check: did a little knot come in too? If it did, see it. Seen, it may loosen. The bell holds the time.
Dhammas, the sense bases. Six doors, eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind, and the fetter that can arise where a sense meets its object.
Your line: the fetter at the door. Today, notice one sense catch you, a smell, a sound, a screen, and see the knot while it's still at the door. Day two hundred sixty-two.

screen: `DAY 262 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: DHAMMAS: THE FACTORS OF AWAKENING.`

fork.reveal: the sutta says the fetter arises dependent on both the sense and its object. that's the moment to see it.

original.note: Pali saṃyojana: a fetter, something that ties you.

trapdoor: what you thought: the senses are the enemy of a spiritual life.
what it means: the senses are doors; the practice is seeing the knot that comes in with what enters.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikāya 10 (Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta), the six sense bases

263.title: Dhammas: the factors of awakening
263.hook: mindfulness, investigation, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, equanimity (MN 10)
263.howItsDone: In Theravada countries the Bojjhanga Sutta is chanted as a protective text (paritta), especially for the sick, and meditation teachers use the seven factors to balance a mind that is too dull or too restless.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dhammas, the sense bases, six doors. Your line was the fetter at the door. Did you catch a knot while it was still at the door? Day two hundred sixty-three.

Three days ago we met the five hindrances, the things that cover a clear mind. It would be easy to think Buddhist practice is mostly about getting rid of bad stuff. But the sutta doesn't stop there. Right after the hindrances and the fetters, it names the good stuff: seven qualities that, when they grow together, carry a person to awakening. If the hindrances are weeds, these are the seeds. Today's word: bojjhanga, the factors of awakening.
screen: `NOT ONLY GETTING RID OF THINGS.` → `IF HINDRANCES ARE WEEDS.` → `THESE ARE THE SEEDS.`

segments.voice: Bojjhanga joins bodhi, awakening, and anga, a limb or factor. The sutta lists seven. First, mindfulness, sati, the one this whole sutta is about. Second, investigation of dhammas: looking closely, with curiosity, at what's happening. Third, energy, viriya, the ardent warmth you met a couple of weeks ago. Fourth, joy, piti, a bright, uplifting gladness. Fifth, tranquility, passaddhi, a calming of body and mind. Sixth, concentration, samadhi, a mind gathered and steady. And seventh, equanimity, upekkha, the same balance that ended the immeasurables a few weeks back. It shows up again here, as the last step. The instruction mirrors the hindrances. If a factor is present, know it's present. If absent, know it's absent. Know how it comes to arise, and how, once arisen, it's brought to fullness. Notice the order. It flows. Mindfulness notices; investigation gets curious; curiosity wakes up energy; energy brightens into joy; joy settles into tranquility; tranquility gathers into concentration; and concentration rests in equanimity. Teachers often say the first three lift a sluggish mind and the last three calm a restless one, with mindfulness useful at every moment. The seven are also chanted. In Theravada countries, the factors are recited for the sick, because a sutta tells of the Buddha reciting them to a monk who was ill, and the monk recovering. People still chant them at hospital bedsides today.
screen: `BODHI + ANGA: LIMBS OF AWAKENING.` · `MINDFULNESS, INVESTIGATION, ENERGY, JOY.` · `TRANQUILITY, CONCENTRATION, EQUANIMITY.` · `ONE FLOWS INTO THE NEXT.` · then, large: `SEVEN FACTORS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Recite the seven slowly to yourself, one per breath, and check each one. Mindfulness: is it here? Investigation: any curiosity? Energy: awake or dull? Joy: even a flicker? Tranquility: is the body calm? Concentration: is the mind gathered? Equanimity: is there balance? Present or absent, just know it. Then say all seven again, and rest. The bell holds the time.
Bojjhanga. The seven factors of awakening, from mindfulness to equanimity, each one flowing into the next.
Your line: seven factors. Today, try saying all seven from memory once, and notice which one feels strongest in you right now. Day two hundred sixty-three.

match.prompt: match each factor to its Pali name.

the sutta also names seven qualities to grow: the factors of awakening.

original.note: Pali bojjhaṅga: a factor, or limb, of awakening.

trapdoor: what you thought: the factors of awakening are rewards you get at the end.
what it means: seven qualities to grow now, each one leading into the next.

what a scholar hears: SN 46.53 gives the balancing advice (investigation, energy, joy for a sluggish mind; tranquility, concentration, equanimity for an excited one), and SN 46.14 tells of the Buddha reciting the factors to the sick Mahākassapa.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikāya 10 (Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta), the seven factors of awakening

264.title: Dhammas: the four truths
264.hook: he knows as it really is: this is dukkha, its arising, its ceasing, the way (MN 10)
264.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often present the four noble truths in the pattern of a physician's diagnosis, and in insight meditation they are contemplated directly in experience rather than only studied as doctrine.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was bojjhanga, and your line was seven factors. Can you still say them? Mindfulness, investigation, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, equanimity. Day two hundred sixty-four.

A good doctor does four things, usually in this order. What's wrong? What's causing it? Can it get better? And what's the treatment? Skip a step and things go badly. Treat the symptom without the cause, and it comes back. Believe it can't get better, and you won't try. Teachers often point out that the Buddha's first teaching has this same shape. And the Satipatthana Sutta, after everything else, ends its tour of the four foundations right back at that first teaching. Today: dhammas, the four truths.
screen: `WHAT'S WRONG? WHAT'S CAUSING IT?` → `CAN IT GET BETTER? WHAT'S THE TREATMENT?` → `THE SHAPE OF THE FIRST TEACHING.`

segments.voice: You met the four noble truths long ago on this path. Here, the sutta turns them into something to watch, not only a teaching to hold. The practitioner knows, as it really is: this is dukkha, the unsatisfactoriness, the stress and pain of life. This is the arising of dukkha. This is the ceasing of dukkha. This is the way leading to its ceasing. As it really is, in Pali yathabhutam, is the key phrase. It means seeing things the way they are, not the way we're afraid they are or wish they were. Notice where the truths come in the sutta. At the very end of the fourth foundation, after the body, feelings, mind, the hindrances, the heaps, the sense bases, and the factors of awakening. It's as if all that watching was training the eyes. Now they can see the biggest pattern of all, right inside ordinary experience. A tight chest before a meeting: this is dukkha. The wanting it to go perfectly: that's its arising. The moment you let go of needing it perfect, and the chest loosens: that's its ceasing, even if only for a moment. And the whole practice you've been learning, the breath, the knowing, the kindness: that's the way. The longer version of the sutta, in the Long Discourses, spells each truth out at length. The shorter one keeps it to four plain lines. Either way, the instruction is the same one this whole part of the path has been practicing: know it, as it is.
screen: `THE FOUR TRUTHS, WATCHED, NOT ONLY BELIEVED.` · `YATHABHUTAM: AS IT REALLY IS.` · `THE BIGGEST PATTERN, SEEN LAST.` · `A TIGHT CHEST IN FOUR STEPS.` · then, large: `KNOW IT AS IT IS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Bring to mind one small problem, not the biggest one. Look at it in four steps. First: what is the discomfort, plainly? Second: what wanting, or not-wanting, is feeding it? Third: can you imagine, even for a breath, that wanting relaxing? What would that feel like? Fourth: what one small, wise step could you take? Then let the problem go, and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Dhammas, the four truths. Dukkha, its arising, its ceasing, and the way: known, as it really is, inside ordinary experience.
Your line: know it as it is. Today, look at one small problem in the four steps: what hurts, what feeds it, what easing would feel like, and one wise step. Day two hundred sixty-four.

screen: `DAY 264 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SEVEN YEARS, OR SEVEN DAYS.`

options: the meeting itself.

fork.reveal: in the four truths, dukkha arises from craving. the wanting feeds the tightness; its easing is the ceasing.

original.note: Pali yathābhūta: as it really is, the way the truths are to be known.

trapdoor: what you thought: the four truths are beliefs you sign up for.
what it means: a pattern you can watch in any small problem, as it really is.

265.title: Seven years, or seven days
265.hook: the promise: practice this way for seven years, or even seven days, and fruit comes (MN 10)
265.howItsDone: Insight meditation retreats in the Theravada world are often run as intensive practice for a set number of days, and some teachers cite the sutta's 'seven days' as encouragement.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dhammas, the four truths. Your line was know it as it is. Did you walk one small problem through the four steps? Day two hundred sixty-five.

Gyms make promises. So do language apps and self-help books. Thirty days to a new you. Fluent in three months. It's easy to get cynical about promises. So it's interesting that this old sutta, after all its careful instructions, ends with a promise of its own. And the way it makes the promise is strange: it starts big and keeps getting smaller, lowering the bar on purpose. Today: seven years, or seven days.
screen: `THIRTY DAYS TO A NEW YOU.` → `THE SUTTA'S OWN PROMISE.` → `STARTING BIG, GETTING SMALLER.`

segments.voice: Here's how the Satipatthana Sutta ends. The Buddha says that if anyone should develop these four foundations in this way for seven years, one of two fruits can be expected. Either final knowledge, awakening, here and now. Or, if some trace of clinging is left, the stage the tradition calls non-return. Then he stops himself. Never mind seven years. Six years. Five. Four, three, two, one. Never mind a year: seven months. Six months, down to one month, half a month. Never mind half a month. If anyone should develop these four foundations for seven days, one of these two fruits can be expected. And then the sutta closes the circle, repeating its opening line: this is the direct path, for the purification of beings. What do you do with a promise like that? The tradition takes it seriously, and also knows that the fruit depends on how deeply one practices, not only on the calendar. The traditional commentary explains that the shorter times apply to people whose practice is already ripe. But there's something any listener can take from the countdown. It's an invitation, not a threat. The Buddha doesn't say, this will take your whole life, so don't bother starting. He keeps lowering the bar, until it's somewhere a person could actually step over it. Seven days is not a lifetime. It's a week. You've already done more than thirty-seven of them on this path.
screen: `SEVEN YEARS: ONE OF TWO FRUITS.` · `SIX, FIVE, FOUR, DOWN TO SEVEN DAYS.` · `BACK TO THE DIRECT PATH.` · `A LOWERED BAR IS AN INVITATION.` · then, large: `EVEN SEVEN DAYS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and rest with the breath for a moment. Then, if you'd like, make a small seven-day promise to yourself. Pick one thing from these weeks: knowing the breath, naming your posture, catching the second arrow, naming a hindrance. Just one. Say it quietly: for seven days, I'll try this. Then let the promise settle, and simply sit with whatever is here. The bell holds the time.
Seven years. The sutta's closing promise: seven years, then fewer and fewer, down to even seven days of this practice, and fruit can be expected.
Your line: even seven days. If you made a seven-day promise, write it down somewhere you'll see it tomorrow morning. Day two hundred sixty-five.

pairs: the line the sutta closes with

options: 'and not a day less.'

trapdoor: what you thought: seven days sounds like a sales pitch.
what it means: an invitation that lowers the bar until anyone can start.
what a scholar hears: the two fruits are aññā (final knowledge, arahantship) or anāgāmitā (non-return); the commentary says the shorter periods apply to those of keener faculties.

266.title: Your four foundations
266.hook: a sitting that moves through body, feeling, mind and dhammas
266.howItsDone: Many practitioners do a sitting that moves through body, feelings, mind and dhammas in turn, and on retreats in the Theravada and insight traditions all four are practiced throughout the day, in sitting, walking and daily tasks.

segments.voice: Yesterday: seven years, or seven days. Your line was even seven days. If you made a small promise, today is day one of it. Day two hundred sixty-six, the last day in the Satipatthana Sutta.

Three weeks ago, we opened the Satipatthana Sutta, the discourse on the foundations of mindfulness. We walked through it one section at a time: the breath, the postures, the bag of grain, the charnel ground, the second arrow, the five visitors, the six doors, the seven factors. Today there's nothing new to learn. Today you get to put the whole thing together, the way it was meant to be used: not as a list, but as one sitting. Today: your four foundations.
screen: `THREE WEEKS IN ONE TEXT.` → `NOTHING NEW TODAY.` → `ONE SITTING, ALL FOUR.`

segments.voice: Here's the whole sutta in one breath. Satipatthana: one way, four doors. The refrain: ardent and gentle. First foundation, the body. Knowing the breath, like the turner at the lathe. The chorus: it arises, it passes. The postures: I know I'm sitting. Clear knowing: even this. The parts: a bag of grain. The elements: four elements. The charnel ground: this body too. Second foundation, feelings: pleasant, painful, neither, and one arrow, not two. Third foundation, the mind: know the mind, and just know it. Fourth foundation, dhammas: the hindrances, it came, it went; five heaps; the fetter at the door; seven factors; and the four truths, know it as it is. And the promise: even seven days. It sounds like a lot. But look at how the four fit together. One way teachers read the order: from the most solid to the most subtle. The body is easy to find: you can always feel your seat. Feelings are a little quicker, a flicker of pleasant or painful. The mind is subtler again, its whole weather. And dhammas are the patterns running through all of it. Each one is a place to stand. On a scattered day, you might only manage the first. On a clear day, you might move through all four. In another sutta, the Buddha calls the four a person's own home ground: a quail caught by a hawk out in the open field is safe again among the clods of its own ploughed field. The practice isn't to master all four at once. It's to know that wherever you are, one of them is right under your feet.

Feelings: what's pleasant here, what's unpleasant, what's neither? Mind: what's the weather, tight or open, scattered or gathered? Dhammas: is a hindrance here, or a factor of awakening, maybe a little calm, a little curiosity? Then rest wherever you find yourself. If you'd like the full version, fifteen minutes, try it some quiet morning this week. The bell holds the time.
Satipatthana, the foundations of mindfulness: one way and four doors, covering the body, feelings, the mind and dhammas, held together in a single sitting.

trapdoor: what you thought: the four foundations are four separate meditations to choose from.

what a scholar hears: the 'solid to subtle' order is a teachers' reading, not the sutta's; the Satipaṭṭhāna Saṃyutta (SN 47) collects many shorter suttas on the four, and SN 47.6 calls them a monk's own ancestral territory.
